{{Short description|Principle in mathematical physics}}

In [[mathematics]] and physics, '''Herglotz's variational principle''', named after German mathematician and physicist [[Gustav Herglotz]], is an extension of the [[Hamilton's principle]], where the Lagrangian L explicitly involves the [[Action (physics)|action]] <math>S</math> as an independent variable, and <math>S</math> itself is represented as the solution of an [[ordinary differential equation|ordinary differential equation (ODE)]] whose right hand side is the Lagrangian {{nowrap|<math>L</math>,}} instead of an integration of {{nowrap|<math>L</math>.}}<ref>{{Citation |last1=Gaset |first1=Jordi |title=The Herglotz variational principle for dissipative field theories |date=2022-11-30 |url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17058 |access-date=2025-05-06 |arxiv=2211.17058 |last2=Lainz |first2=Manuel |last3=Mas |first3=Arnau |last4=Rivas |first4=Xavier|journal=Geometric Mechanics |volume=01 |issue=2 |pages=153–178 |doi=10.1142/S2972458924500060 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite report |url=https://projecteuclid.org/ebooks/geometry-integrability-and-quantization/Proceedings-of-the-Twelfth-International-Conference-on-Geometry-Integrability-and/chapter/The-Variational-Principle-of-Hergloz-and-Related-Results/10.7546/giq-12-2011-214-225 |title=The Variational Principle of Hergloz and Related Results |last=Georgieva |first=Bogdana |date=2012 |publisher=GIQ |doi=10.7546/giq-12-2011-214-225}}</ref> Herglotz's variational principle is known as the variational principle for nonconservative [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrange equations]] and [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamilton equations]]. It was first proposed in the context of [[contact geometry]].

== Mathematical formulation ==
This presentation is from <ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Guenther |first1=R. B. |url=https://www.tmna.ncu.pl/static/files/LNNA_01.pdf |title=The Herglotz Lectures on Contact Transformations and Hamiltonian Systems |last2=Gottsch |first2=J. A. |last3=Guenther |first3=C. M. |date=1996 |publisher=Juliusz Center for Nonlinear Studies |location=Toruń, Poland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230802135803/https://www.tmna.ncu.pl/static/files/LNNA_01.pdf |archive-date=2 Aug 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=|pages=108-114}}

=== Hamilton's principle ===
As in Lagrangian mechanics, we consider a system with <math>n</math> degrees of freedom. Let <math>\boldsymbol q = (q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n)</math> be its [[generalized coordinates]], and let <math>\boldsymbol u = (u_1, u_2, \dots, u_n)</math> be its generalized velocity. Let <math>L = L(t,\boldsymbol{q}, \boldsymbol{u})</math> be the Lagrangian function of the [[physical system]]. Let <math>S</math> be the [[Action (physics)|action]].

Lagrangian mechanics is derived using Hamilton's principle. Fix a starting time and configuration <math>t_0, \boldsymbol  q_0</math> and an ending time and configuration {{nowrap|<math>t_1, \boldsymbol  q_1</math>.}} Hamilton's principle states that physically real trajectories from are the solutions to the problem of variational calculus:<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\delta \int_\gamma L(t, \gamma(t), \dot\gamma(t)) dt = 0 \\
\gamma \text{ has end points } t_0, \boldsymbol  q_0, t_1, \boldsymbol  q_1
\end{cases}</math>Equivalently, it can be formulated as<math display="block" id="1">\begin{cases}
\delta S(t_1) = 0\\
\dot S (t) = L(t, \gamma (t), \dot \gamma (t)), & t \in [t_0, t_1] \\
S(t_0) = S_0 \\
\gamma \text{ has end points } t_0, \boldsymbol  q_0, t_1, \boldsymbol  q_1
\end{cases}</math>

=== Herglotz's variational principle ===
Herglotz's variational principle simply generalizes by allowing the Lagrangian to depend on the action as well. It is of form {{nowrap|<math>L = L(t,\boldsymbol{q}, \boldsymbol{u},S)</math>,}} depending on <math>2n+2</math> variables.
<math display="block" id="1">\begin{cases}
\delta S(t_1) = 0\\
\dot S (t) = L(t, \gamma (t), \dot \gamma (t), S(t)), & t \in [t_0, t_1] \\
S(t_0) = S_0 \\
\gamma \text{ has end points } t_0, \boldsymbol  q_0, t_1, \boldsymbol  q_1
\end{cases}</math>

=== Euler–Lagrange–Herglotz equation ===
Hamilton's variational principle gives the [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler–Langrange equations]].<math display="block">\frac{d}{d t} \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \boldsymbol q}\right) 
 - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol q} = 0</math> Similarly, Herglotz's variational principle gives the Euler–Lagrange–Herglotz equations
<math display="block">\frac{d}{d t} \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \boldsymbol q}\right) 
 - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol q} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial S} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \boldsymbol q}</math> which involves an extra term <math display="inline">\frac{\partial L}{\partial S} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \boldsymbol q}</math> that can describe the dissipation of the system. The original Euler–Langrange equations are recovered as a special case when {{nowrap|<math>\partial_S L = 0</math>.}}

=== Hamiltonian form ===
Similar to how Lagrangian mechanics is equivalent to Hamiltonian mechanics, the Lagrangian form of Herglotz principle is equivalent to a Hamiltonian form.

Define the momentum and Hamiltonian by taking a [[Legendre transformation]]<math display="block">p_i := \frac{\partial L}{\partial u_i}, \quad H := \sum_i p_i u_i - L</math> Then the equations of motion are<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \dot q_i = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} \\[1ex]
\displaystyle \dot p_i = -\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i} + p_i \frac{\partial H}{\partial S}\right) \\[1ex]
\displaystyle \dot S = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} - H
\end{cases}</math>

=== Hamilton–Jacobi equation ===
If <math>S(t, q)</math> is written as a function of time and configuration, then it satisfies a [[Hamilton–Jacobi equation]]<math display="block">dS = -H\,dt + \sum_i p_i \, dq^i</math>

== Derivation ==
In order to solve this minimization problem, we impose a variation <math>\delta \boldsymbol q</math> on {{nowrap|<math>\boldsymbol q</math>,}} and suppose <math>S(t)</math> undergoes a variation <math>\delta S(t)</math> correspondingly, then<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\delta \dot S(t) & = L (t, \boldsymbol q (t) + \delta \boldsymbol q (t), \dot \boldsymbol q(t) + \delta \dot \boldsymbol q (t), S(t) + \delta S(t)) - L (t, \boldsymbol q (t), \dot \boldsymbol q(t), S(t)) \\
& = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol q} \delta \boldsymbol q(t) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \boldsymbol q} \delta \dot \boldsymbol q(t) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial S} \delta S(t)
\end{aligned}
</math> and since the [[initial condition]] is not changed, {{nowrap|<math>\delta S_0 = 0</math>.}} The above equation a linear ODE for the function {{nowrap|<math>\delta S(t)</math>,}} and it can be solved by introducing an [[integrating factor]] {{nowrap|<math display="inline">\mu (t) = \exp\left(\int_{t_0}^t \frac{\partial L}{\partial S} dt\right)</math>,}} which is uniquely determined by the ODE <math display="block">\dot{\mu }( t) =-\mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}, \quad u(t_0) = 1.</math>By multiplying <math>\mu(t)</math> on both sides of the equation of <math>\delta \dot S</math> and moving the term <math display="inline">\mu (t) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S} \delta S(t)
</math> to the left hand side, we get
<math display="block">\mu ( t) \delta \dot{S}( t) -\mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial S} \delta S( t) =\mu ( t)\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t) +\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} \delta \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}( t)\right).
</math>
Note that, since {{nowrap|<math display="inline">\dot{\mu }( t) =-\mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}</math>,}} the left hand side equals to <math display="block">\mu ( t) \delta \dot{S}( t) +\dot{\mu }( t) \delta S( t) =\frac{d( \mu ( t) \delta S( t))}{d t}</math>and therefore we can do an integration of the equation above from <math>t=t_0</math> to {{nowrap|<math>t=t_1</math>,}} yielding <math display="block">\mu ( t_1) \delta S_1 -\mu ( t_0) \delta S_0 =\int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t) +\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} \delta \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}( t)\right)d t</math> where the <math>\delta S_0 = 0</math> so the left hand side actually only contains one term <math>\mu(t_1) \delta S_1</math>, and for the right hand side, we can perform the integration-by-part on the <math display="inline">\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} \delta \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}( t)</math> term to remove the [[time derivative]] on {{nowrap|<math display="inline">\delta \boldsymbol{q}</math>:}}
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
 & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t) +\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} \delta \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}( t)\right)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t+\int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} \delta \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}( t)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t+\mu ( t_1)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\underbrace{\delta {\boldsymbol{q}}( t_1)}_{=0} -\mu ( t_0)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\underbrace{\delta {\boldsymbol{q}}( t_0)}_{=0} -\int _{t_0}^{t_1}\frac{d}{d t}\left( \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right) \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t-\int _{t_0}^{t_1}\frac{d}{d t}\left( \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right) \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t-\int _{t_0}^{t_1}\left(\dot{\mu }( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} +\mu ( t)\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right) \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t-\int _{t_0}^{t_1}\left( -\mu ( t)\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} +\mu ( t)\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right) \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t\\
= & \int _{t_0}^{t_1} \mu ( t)\underline{\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{q}} +\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}} -\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right)} \delta \boldsymbol{q}( t)d t,
\end{aligned}</math>
and when <math> S_1</math> is minimized, <math> \delta S_1 = 0</math> for all {{nowrap|<math> \delta \boldsymbol q</math>,}} which indicates that the underlined term in the last line of the equation above has to be zero on the entire interval {{nowrap|<math>[t_0, t_1]</math>,}} this gives rise to the Euler–Lagrange–Herglotz equation.

== Noether's theorem ==
Generalizations of [[Noether's theorem]] and [[Noether's second theorem]] apply to Herglotz's variational principle.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Georgieva |first1=Bogdana |last2=Guenther |first2=Ronald |date=2002 |title=First Noether-type theorem for the generalized variational principle of Herglotz |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/topological-methods-in-nonlinear-analysis/volume-20/issue-2/First-Noether-type-theorem-for-the-generalized-variational-/tmna/1470081175.full |journal=Topological Methods in Nonlinear Analysis |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=261–273 |mr=1962221 |zbl=1032.58007}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last=Georgieva |first=Bogdana A. |title=Noether-type theorems for the generalized variational principle of Herglotz |date=2001 |type=PhD thesis |publisher=Oregon State University |url=https://ir.library.oregonstate.edu/downloads/jq085n51c}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Georgieva |first1=Bogdana |last2=Guenther |first2=Ronald B. |date=2005 |title=Second Noether-type theorem for the generalized variational principle of Herglotz |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/topological-methods-in-nonlinear-analysis/volume-26/issue-2/Second-Noether-type-theorem-for-the-generalized/tmna/1466705574.full |journal=Topological Methods in Nonlinear Analysis |publisher=Juliusz Schauder Center for Nonlinear Studies |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=307–314 |mr=2197762 |zbl=1191.70007}}</ref>

An [[infinitesimal transformation]] is<math display="block">\bar t = t + \varepsilon T(t, q), \quad \bar q  = q + \varepsilon Q(t, q)</math> where <math>T, Q</math> are smooth functions of time and configuration, and <math>\varepsilon</math> is an infinitesimal. The transformation deforms a trajectory <math>(t, q(t))</math> to {{nowrap|<math>(t + \varepsilon T(t, q), q(t) + \varepsilon Q(t, q))</math>,}} and accordingly deforms the action integral as well.

We say that the infinitesimal transformation is a symmetry of the action iff the change in <math>S(t_1) - S(t_0)</math> under the infinitesimal transformation is order {{nowrap|<math>O(\varepsilon^2)</math>.}} Given such an infinitesimal symmetry, the quantity is a [[constant of motion]]<math display="block">\exp\left(-\int_{t_0}^{t} \frac{\partial L(t')}{\partial S} \, dt'\right) \left[T {\left(L - \dot q \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} \right)} + Q \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} \right]</math> where <math>\partial_S L(t') </math> is more explicitly written as<math display="block">\partial_S L(t', q(t'), \dot q(t'), S(t'))</math> There is also a version for [[multiple time dimensions]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Georgieva |first=Bogdana |last2=Guenther |first2=Ronald |last3=Bodurov |first3=Theodore |date=2003-09-01 |title=Generalized variational principle of Herglotz for several independent variables. First Noether-type theorem |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/44/9/3911/440504/Generalized-variational-principle-of-Herglotz-for |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=44 |issue=9 |pages=3911–3927 |doi=10.1063/1.1597419 |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Damped particle on a line ===
The motion of a particle of mass <math>m</math> in a potential field <math>V</math> with [[damping coefficient]] <math>\gamma</math> is<math display="block">m \ddot x = -V'(x) - \gamma \dot x.</math>It can be produced as the Euler–Lagrange–Herglotz for<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=114}}<math display="block">L(t,x,\dot x,S) = \tfrac{1}{2} m \dot x^2 - V(x) -\gamma S</math>

=== A more general particle on a line ===
More generally, consider a particle on a line under the influence of 3 forces: a [[conservative force]] due to a potential field, a dissipative force proportional to {{nowrap|<math>\dot x</math>,}} and another force proportional to {{nowrap|<math>\dot x^2</math>.}} Write it as<ref name=":1" />
<math display="block">\ddot{x}+f(x) \dot{x}^2+g(t) \dot{x} + h(x) = 0</math>
This equation is the Euler–Lagrange–Herglotz equation for the Lagrangian
<math display="block"> L = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{x}^2 - \left[2 f(x) \dot{x} + g(t)\right] S - U(x) </math>
where <math display="inline">U(x)</math> is any solution of the [[Ordinary differential equation|ODE]]
<math display="block">
\frac{dU(x)}{dx} + 2 f(x) U(x) = h(x) .
</math>Some important special cases: 

* When <math> f(x) = 0 </math> and <math> g(t) </math> is constant, it is the damped harmonic oscillator given above.
* When <math display="inline">h(x)=x^n, f(x)=0</math> and <math display="inline">g(t)=2 / t</math>, it is the [[Lane–Emden equation]]<math display="block">
\ddot{x}+\frac{2}{t} \dot{x}+x^n=0, \quad n \neq-1 .
</math> with Lagrangian <math display="block">
L=\frac{1}{2} \dot{x}^2-\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}-\frac{2}{t} z .
</math>
* When <math display="inline">h(x)=0</math>, it is a Rayleigh-type system<math display="block">\ddot{x}+f(x) \dot{x}^2+g(t) \dot{x}=0 .</math> with Lagrangian<math display="block">
L = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{x}^2 - \left[2 f(x) \dot{x} + g(t)\right] z .
</math>
